summary: In Greek mythology, Apis (Ancient Greek Ἆπις) is an early king of Argos, son of Phoroneus by the nymph Teledice and brother of Niobe. He turns his father's kingship into a tyranny, names the Peloponnese Apia after himself, and dies childless in a conspiracy — after which the land-name and succession pass toward Argus son of Zeus and Niobe.
attribution: Adapted from Wikipedia, "Apis (Greek mythology)" · CC BY-SA 4.0
etymology: Greek Ἆπις; the Peloponnese as "Apia" commemorates his name. Distinct from the Egyptian bull-god Apis, though some ancient strands give Peloponnesian Apis an Egyptian colouring.

sections.heading: Phoroneid tyrant
paragraphs: Apollodorus makes Apis son of Phoroneus and Teledice. During his reign he establishes a tyrannical government and calls the peninsula Apia; he is killed in a conspiracy headed by Thelxion of Sparta and Telchis, and dies without children.

Aeschylus' Suppliants knows another Apis — a Naupactian seer-healer, son of Apollo, who frees Argos from earth-born snakes — and Apollodorus sometimes confounds namesakes. The atlas id apis-phoroneus is the Phoroneid king of the tyrannical Apia strand alone.

sections.heading: Homonyms
paragraphs: Do not merge him with Apis king of Sicyon son of Telchis, with Aeschylus' healer, with Apis son of Jason of Pallantium, or with the Egyptian sacred bull.
